title: Head Tracking
description: A head tracking camera glues the lens to the skull so the face stays pinned while the background orbits. The head is the tripod; turns shear the room.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The face is the only stable point. Disorientation, intimacy, a character who cannot see the room changing: the world slides around a pinned portrait.
A close-up that pans with them from far away is not glued. Snorricam is chest-mounted and sees the body; head tracking pins the face.
Turns must sweep the background.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Helmet rig, face mount, or a digital lock to the skull. Face sharp, no extra zoom.
When they turn, the room orbits. Prompt: Head-tracking camera on [Subject], the lens glued to the skull, background sliding as the face stays pinned.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when the face must stay while the world becomes weather. Do not use a long-lens pan and claim a lock.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a close-up panned from a distance. The tell: the face drifts in frame, or the background does not shear on a turn.
The fix: lock to the skull, pin the face, let the room orbit.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Head Tracking in film?
Head tracking glues the camera to the skull so the face stays pinned while the background orbits as the person turns.
Head Tracking vs SnorriCam
Snorricam is typically chest-mounted and sees the body in the world. Head tracking pins the face; the skull is the tripod.
When should I use Head Tracking?
Use it for disorientation or intimacy when the face is the only stable point. Do not fake it with a long-lens pan.
How do I prompt Head Tracking for AI image or video?
Write a camera locked to the head, face sharp, world sliding. Example: Head-tracking camera on [Subject], the lens glued to the skull, background sliding as the face stays pinned.
